about: The Prologue of Saint John (John 1:1–14), read at the Gospel side at the end of Mass. Before reading, the priest signs the altar or book and then his forehead, lips, and breast. He genuflects at “Et Verbum caro factum est”.

seg.nr: Then the priest, at the Gospel side with hands joined, says:
And signing with the sign of the cross first the altar or the book, then himself on the forehead, the lips and the breast, the priest says:

seg.tr: The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John.

seg.nr: With his hands joined the priest continues:

seg.tr: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made. In Him was life, and the life was the Light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.

ex.w018: “Verbum” renders Greek λόγος and names the eternal Son of God, the Word.

nt.w036: The gender is open. The only grammatical antecedent is Verbum, which is neuter, but the tradition reads a masculine here, of the Person. This edition takes the masculine.
nt.w041: The gender is open, as at w036. This edition takes the masculine.
nt.w049: The gender is open, as at w036. This edition takes the masculine.

seg.tr: There was a man sent from God whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the Light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the Light, but came to bear witness to the Light.

ex.w077: Spelled like the present, read as the perfect: the narrative runs in the past — “Fuit” (w067), “erat” (w074) — and long “vēnit” is the perfect.

seg.tr: There was the true Light, which enlightens every man coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him. He came to His own, but His own did not receive Him. But to all who received Him, He gave power to become sons of God: to those who believe in His name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth; and we saw His glory—glory such as belongs to the Father's Only-begotten Son.

ex.w184: “Plenum” can be nominative or accusative. This edition reads it as a nominative referring to “Verbum” (w167), whereas the Glossa interlinearis reads an accusative object of “vídimus”.

nt.w184: The form decides nothing between nominative and accusative, and the old commentators read it both ways. This edition takes the nominative and marks the doubt.
